newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress unlikely to bail out DC soon - aide.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress unlikely to bail out DC soon - aide.

text.p: The U.S. Congress will not consider bailing the District of Columbia out of some of its most costly programs until the city spells out exactly what it wants Capitol Hill to do and further pares down its bloated budget, a key U.S. House aide said on Thursday.
Ron Hamm, staff director of the House Government Reform Committee's D.C. subpanel, added, however, that Congress may be ready in about 12 months to begin debating the volatile issue.

Hamm was responding to a controversial D.C. control board report due out later today that says Congress must take over some of the financial burden of D.C. programs, including possibly Medicaid, mental health care, road and bridge maintenance and prisons.
A draft of the report, which says the control board will send Congress recommendations by March 31, was obtained by Reuters on Wednesday.

"They intend to come up here by March 31 with the recommendation that the federal government assume up to a billion dollars of operational costs, whether or not the District is being run effectively," Hamm said in a telephone interview.
But Congress may be ready in about a year to debate the takeover issue if the city provides detailed documentation of where it needs critical help, Hamm said.

"It would not be unreasonable to expect that, working in consultation with the Congress and federal executive (branch), the picture may become clearer as to what may be possible at the federal level" within a year, Hamm said.
"They are essentially saying that it's time to act," Hamm continued. "We applaud that. We look forward to seeing those things go forward."
But it is not going to happen in six months, Hamm said. "They have told us there are tens of millions of dollars of wasteful spending in the District," Hamm said.

"Until we are able to study whether the city is as seriously out of balance as it claims to be, Congress is (not) going to reach in and grab hundreds of millions of dollars" from federal coffers, Hamm said.
Hamm said another problem is that the federal government has no bureaucracy in place to take over Medicaid, health care or other programs.

"(It) could not just swoop in and pick up the operations" of a mental health program, for instance, Hamm said. "We don't have any agency to do it. Are they proposing we spend even more money to set up a bureaucracy when we are trying to shrink the federal government?"
Hamm added that the control board report ignores the fact that D.C. is one of the few U.S. cities that can levy income and sales taxes, and the city does so at "very high rates."
